case_study_insert.main_stem: Wave Ridge Hotels (WRH) is a private limited company in the hospitality sector, operating boutique coastal hotels and employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2012 by Nadia Okoro, WRH runs a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership, giving reception and housekeeping teams a say in service routines. WRH plans to invest $720,000 in a new 60-room boutique wing with energy-efficient fittings, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $25 a unit and a selling price of $85, and currently produces 12,000 units a year, each a booked room-night. WRH faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 18% among housekeeping staff and guest complaints about room cleanliness are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Guest Services Report — Q3 2025: WRH recorded 3,000 room-nights last quarter at an average occupancy of 78%, down from 84% a year earlier. Room-cleanliness complaints rose to 46 per month from 29. Online review score fell to 4.1 from 4.5 out of 5. Average check-in time is 6.4 minutes. A survey of 500 guests found that 68% would pay up to $6 more for a certified eco-friendly room, and 57% choose hotels using renewable energy. Staff records show 11 of 30 employees have not completed on-the-job training in hygiene; off-the-job training refresher courses at the local college cost $260 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Wave Ridge Hotels as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (October 2026): (1) The central bank lifted the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, raising borrowing costs on WRH's variable-rate bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.50 to $13.23 per hour, increasing the wage bill for WRH's 30 housekeeping and reception staff. (3) Hotel energy and laundry input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year, while domestic tourism spending grew 4.2% and local room occupancy rose 2.0 percentage points.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for WRH of funding the new 60-room wing with a $450,000 bank loan rather than using only retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $450,000 ten-year bank loan lets WRH complete the $720,000 wing now rather than waiting years to accumulate that sum from 12,000 room-nights a year at $85. Opening the 60 rooms sooner brings forward revenue that helps absorb fixed costs of $180,000 a year, and the loan is repaid over the same years the rooms earn. Keeping the $270,000 retained profit untouched also preserves cash for the rising trade receivables and inventories seen in Appendix 2, instead of locking every dollar into non-current assets.

Point 2: Borrowing matches the cost of the wing to the stream of room-night income it creates. With a contribution of $60 a room-night and break-even of only 3,000 room-nights, WRH has a margin of safety of 9,000 room-nights over its current 12,000, so the loan is comfortably serviceable. Holding $270,000 retained profit back gives a reserve if labour turnover of 18% forces extra recruitment or hygiene training at $260 per employee. A bank loan therefore accelerates growth while retained profit cushions the very operational problems WRH currently faces.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a bank loan over retained profit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to WRH's $720,000 wing, room-night economics and operational problems.

questions.question_text: WRH is launching its new 60-room wing. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should WRH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A TV campaign reaches a mass audience quickly and could build awareness of the 60-room wing across the whole country. For a boutique coastal hotel group, however, most viewers live far from WRH's properties and cannot easily book, so much of the spend is wasted. Production and airtime costs would also be severe for a business with fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a $450,000 loan to service.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is far cheaper and can target listeners near WRH's coastal hotels with time-sensitive launch messages. Its weakness is reach: WRH's 68% of 500 surveyed guests willing to pay $6 more for eco-friendly rooms are not confined to one local radio area, and a 30-employee operator needs bookings from across the country to fill 12,000 room-nights a year.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel and lifestyle influencers can show the energy-efficient rooms directly to the 57% of surveyed guests who choose hotels using renewable energy, with measurable engagement at a fraction of TV cost. Results build more slowly than television and depend on influencer credibility, but the message can be tracked and targeted nationally.

Recommendation: WRH should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact eco-conscious segment in the survey, scales nationally unlike local radio, and costs far less than television while reinforcing the $6 premium positioning. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, and radio is rejected as too geographically narrow for a group seeking to raise occupancy from 78%. The campaign can also be paused quickly if bookings do not rise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal reference to WRH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to WRH's launch.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in WRH's context with a justified recommendation that explains why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: WRH's labour turnover has reached 18% and cleanliness complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for WRH of using democratic leadership to improve staff motivation.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives WRH's 30 reception and housekeeping employees a real voice in how rooms are cleaned and inspected, which supports their social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Staff who help design cleaning checklists are more likely to take pride in the work, directly tackling the 46 cleanliness complaints a month and protecting the 4.1 review score. In a flat structure, ideas reach Nadia Okoro quickly, so improvements can be made without delay.

Point 2: Consulting the team improves the quality of decisions because the people cleaning the rooms know which areas need more time or better equipment. Greater involvement builds commitment and should reduce the 18% labour turnover, saving the recruitment and $260 per employee hygiene-training costs. Stable staff also protect the 12,000 room-nights a year and the $60 contribution on each, making the $450,000 loan easier to service while the 60-room wing beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to WRH's turnover, complaints and training costs.

questions.question_text: WRH must train 11 housekeeping staff in new hygiene procedures. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should WRH choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training beside experienced housekeepers is directly relevant to WRH's own rooms and cleanliness standards, costs no course fees and keeps all 11 staff productive while they learn. This protects the 3,000 room-nights handled last quarter and attacks the 46 monthly complaints at source. The drawbacks are that trainers are themselves working staff, so service can slow, and bad habits may be passed on unless supervisors inspect carefully; formal certification is also limited if guests demand proof of hygiene standards.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $260 per employee gives structured, up-to-date hygiene knowledge and a recognised certificate for all 11 staff, costing $2,860 in total — small beside the $720,000 investment. It removes staff from the floor, however, reducing short-term room availability when occupancy is already 78%, and generic content may not match WRH's exact room-turnover routines, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: WRH should choose on-the-job training first, with short college refresher sessions later. It is cheaper, room-specific and avoids losing 11 staff from a 30-person workforce while complaints are high; full off-the-job training is rejected because the disruption would cut room-nights and the $260 per head cost duplicates skills already held in-house. Managers should monitor the 46 complaints and 4.1 review score weekly, and supervisors should inspect rooms daily so bad habits cannot spread. If complaints do not fall after four weeks, a short college certificate course for the 11 staff should be funded from retained profit rather than delaying the $720,000 wing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to WRH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of WRH's complaints and staffing.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to WRH's hygiene problem.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WRH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($85 − $25) = $180,000 ÷ $60 = 3,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 3,000 room-nights a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $85 − $25 = $60. Answer: contribution per unit is $60.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WRH's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 3,000-unit break-even with actual output of 12,000 room-nights: the margin of safety is 9,000 room-nights, showing the 60-room wing can be filled well above break-even and helping decide when to phase in the new rooms.
2. Use the $60 contribution to model pricing, for example a $6 eco-friendly premium would raise contribution to $66 and could be tested against the 68% of surveyed guests willing to pay it.
3. Check loan affordability: 3,000 break-even room-nights against 12,000 sold shows the $450,000 loan can be serviced, and managers can set monthly room-night targets to protect that cushion.
4. Benchmark unit cost: $180,000 ÷ 12,000 units + $25 = $40 a room-night, which can be tracked each quarter to spot waste or the effect of the 9.5% energy-cost rise before it erodes the $60 contribution.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 3,000 room-nights | (ii) Contribution per unit = $60 | (iii) Four uses: margin of safety against 12,000 room-nights, pricing/eco-premium modelling, $450,000 loan feasibility and $40 unit-cost benchmarking.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WRH's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has WRH's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.73 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.10 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $30,000 inventories + $90,000 trade receivables + $20,000 cash = $140,000. 2025 current assets = $25,000 + $120,000 + $45,000 = $190,000. 2024: $140,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.40; 2025: $190,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.73. Excluding inventories: 2024 ($140,000 − $30,000) ÷ $100,000 = $110,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.10; 2025 ($190,000 − $25,000) ÷ $110,000 = $165,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.50.

Evaluation: Liquidity strengthened clearly. The first measure rose from 1.40 to 1.73 as current assets increased while current liabilities rose only from $100,000 to $110,000. The second measure, which strips out inventories, rose from 1.10 to 1.50, so the improvement does not depend on selling stock — important when WRH is funding a $720,000 wing. Cash rose from $20,000 to $45,000, giving a real buffer for the $450,000 loan. However, trade receivables grew from $90,000 to $120,000, tying up cash; if corporate clients pay late the stronger position could quickly weaken, so credit control must tighten.

Conclusion: WRH's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the rise is backed by more cash rather than stock, so short-term solvency is genuinely better. The residual risk is rising receivables, which should be managed before the new wing absorbs more cash. The $270,000 retained profit going into the wing should also be replenished before further borrowing, because cash of $45,000 is a limited buffer against a $450,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WRH of introducing certified eco-friendly rooms in the new wing.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 500 guests found that 68% would pay up to $6 more for a certified eco-friendly room and 57% already choose hotels using renewable energy. That supports a premium on the $85 price, lifting contribution above $60 a room-night and helping cover the $180,000 fixed costs and the $450,000 loan. Certification also differentiates the 60-room wing from competitors and may raise the 78% occupancy rate.

Disadvantage: Certification and eco-friendly materials typically cost more than standard fittings, which could push the $25 variable cost per room-night upward and squeeze the $60 margin unless the full $6 premium is accepted. If guests question the certification or the rooms fail inspection, the 4.1 review score and the 46 cleanliness complaints could worsen, and the $720,000 investment might not earn the expected return. Guests who value sustainability may also rate WRH more highly, protecting the 4.1 review score as the 60 new rooms open and helping justify the $85 price.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using WRH's survey, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in energy and laundry input costs will affect WRH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If WRH's $450,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $180,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates could also make guests more cautious about discretionary coastal breaks and raise the cost of future borrowing, but WRH can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.23 per hour): With a workforce of 30 in housekeeping and reception, the rise feeds directly into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no honest annual total can be invented; the defensible test is productivity: 12,000 room-nights ÷ 30 staff = 400 room-nights per worker. If productivity holds, the extra wage cost is spread across more output; if labour turnover of 18% disrupts service, unit labour cost rises and the $60 contribution shrinks.

Input cost inflation (9.5% energy and laundry): The $25 variable cost per room-night is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is defensible: if the entire $25 rose 9.5%, that is 0.095 × $25 = $2.38 a room-night, and at 12,000 room-nights about $28,560 a year. Even a smaller increase compounds on every room-night sold and directly erodes the $60 contribution that justifies the $720,000 wing. The $6 eco-friendly premium can recover part of it, but not all.

Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in energy and laundry costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 12,000 room-nights and strikes at the $60 contribution that services the loan, whereas the rate rise adds a bounded $3,375 a year and the wage rise can be offset if the 400 room-nights per worker productivity is maintained.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to WRH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on WRH's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in WRH's context with a justified greatest-impact judgment and reasons why the others are smaller.
